title: Write-Behind
subtitle: Asynchronous write-back caching for absorbing extreme write bursts via batching and write coalescing.
keyTakeaways: In Write-Behind (Write-Back) caching, applications write solely to in-memory cache and receive immediate sub-millisecond acknowledgments.
An asynchronous worker flushes dirty cache entries to the database in batches, coalescing repeated updates to the same row into a single database write.
The primary trade-off is durability risk: if the cache node crashes or loses power before dirty entries flush to disk, unpersisted writes are permanently lost.

sections.heading: Write Coalescing and Batch Persistence Mechanics
sections.body: In high-throughput write workloads like video view counters, game leaderboards, or live voting systems, issuing a SQL `UPDATE` statement for every single increment creates massive lock contention and saturates database disk IOPS. Write-Behind caching solves this by acknowledging writes in memory within microseconds and batching disk persistence in the background.
bullets: Write Coalescing: If a YouTube video receives 10,000 views in 5 seconds, an in-memory counter increments 10,000 times in Redis. The asynchronous worker flushes a single `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 10000 WHERE id = 1` to the database, cutting database write IOPS by 99.9%.
Decoupled Latency: API response times are completely decoupled from database disk write speeds, connection pool limits, or transient database stalls.
Traffic Smoothing: Absorbs massive flash sales or viral events without overwhelming backing relational databases.

sections.heading: Managing Durability Risks and Crash Recovery
sections.body: The defining liability of Write-Behind caching is the window of vulnerability between memory admission and disk persistence. If a cache instance crashes, suffers an OOM kill, or reboots during that window, all unwritten state is gone forever.
bullets: Write-Ahead Log (WAL) Durability: Mitigate loss by appending mutations to an append-only log or Redis Stream before acknowledging the client.
Bounded Flush Windows: Enforce strict limits on both time (flush every 5 seconds) and queue size (flush when buffer reaches 1,000 records) to bound maximum possible loss.
Applicability Boundary: Never use Write-Behind for financial ledger transactions, order placements, or identity state where data loss is unacceptable.

tradeOffs.pros: Highest possible write throughput; sub-millisecond API response latency; reduces database write IOPS by 90%+ via coalescing.
tradeOffs.cons: Risk of permanent data loss on cache node failure; complex operational recovery and ordering guarantees.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time view counters, GPS telemetry tracking, high-frequency IoT metrics, and voting systems.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero data loss; ACID transactional integrity preserved; straightforward failure recovery.
tradeOffs.cons: Write throughput bounded by database disk IOPS; client latency includes database round-trip time.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Payment transactions, e-commerce orders, password changes, and inventory bookings.

interviewTip: Propose Write-Behind when designing high-volume counter systems (such as a YouTube view counter or Reddit upvote tracker): 'Because view counts do not require strict financial consistency and individual views can be coalesced, we will use Write-Behind caching with Redis. We buffer increments in memory and flush batched updates to the database every 10 seconds, cutting database write load by 99%.'
